title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems

paper.title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
paper.abstract:
Abstract Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images.
Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points.
We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes.
Extensive experiments on CelebA ( 128 × 128 128\times 128 ) and AFHQ ( 256 × 256 256\times 256 ) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.
Code is available in https://github.com/nzilberstein/Flow-map-denoisers

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image restoration is a highly ill-posed inverse problem: a single degraded observation can correspond to a vast set of plausible clean images. Standard regression approaches that minimize mean squared error (MSE) approximate the conditional expectation ( Ongie et al., 2020 ) , achieving minimum distortion at the cost of over-smoothed reconstructions that lack fine detail. In contrast, posterior sampling techniques ( Kawar et al., 2021 ) produce realistic-looking solutions at the cost of higher distortion. This inherent compromise is formalized by the distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff ( Blau and Michaeli, 2018 ; Freirich et al., 2021 ) . Because the ideal balance between low distortion and high perceptual quality is strictly user-dependent, designing a single model capable of traversing the DP plane at inference time remains a central challenge in computational imaging. Most existing methods commit to a single operating point in the DP plane , either targeting minimum distortion through supervised regression ( Dong et al., 2015 ; Terris et al., 2026 ) , or minimum perception by leveraging recent generative models as priors ( Pokle et al., 2024 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Kadkhodaie and Simoncelli, 2021 ) to draw samples from the posterior. A few recent works based on data-dependent flow models aim to traverse the DP plane ( Ohayon et al., 2025 ; Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2024 ) , by explicitly interpolating between measurement-dependent estimators (e.g., the conditional mean) and the clean image. Unlike these approaches, which require external mechanisms, such as interpolation, discretization choices, or retraining, to move along the DP frontier, we show that this tradeoff is already implicitly encoded in the dynamics of flow maps. This raises the question of whether this behavior can be achieved without relying on solver choices, such as increasing the number of discretization steps. In this work, we propose a unified approach based on flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025b ; Boffi et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025b ) , which unifies all operating points along the DP plane within a single model. While prior work primarily uses flow maps to accelerate sampling ( Gülle et al., 2026 ; Sabour et al., 2025a ; Spagnoletti et al., 2025 ) , we instead leverage them to traverse the DP frontier . Our key observation is that the lookahead t t selects a point along a continuum of estimators—termed average denoisers —implicitly encoded within a single trained flow map, thus acting as a knob to control the characteristics of the restored image. This perspective reveals DP control as an intrinsic property of the learned flow map, eliminating the need for multiple models, auxiliary networks, or heuristic solver choices. This family spans the entire DP frontier, recovering the MMSE estimator at one extreme and approaching posterior sampling at the other. For Gaussian targets, we prove that this family spans the entire DP frontier, recovering the MMSE estimator at one extreme and approaching posterior sampling at the other, tracing the optimal DP curve ( Freirich et al., 2021 ) . While this exact theoretical correspondence strictly holds for Gaussian noise problems, we empirically observe similar behavior for natural images. When extending this approach to general, non-Gaussian inverse problems, traversing the lookahead serves as an approximation to the true DP frontier; here, the lookahead controls a tradeoff that combines perceptual alignment with data-consistency effects, rather than exactly reproducing the denoising DP frontier. By embedding these denoisers within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) framework ( Venkatakrishnan et al., 2013 ) , we leverage this property to obtain a versatile solver that effectively traverses the DP frontier across a wide range of inverse problems. Fig. 1 illustrates this behavior on a 2D Gaussian mixture model. Overall, our contributions are: • Flow maps as a continuum of DP estimators. We reinterpret flow maps as a family of denoisers indexed by a lookahead parameter t t , enabling continuous traversal of the DP plane with a single model. • Exact optimality in the Gaussian case. We show that this family recovers the optimal DP curve for Gaussian targets, establishing a direct link between flow maps and DP theory. • PnP reconstruction with continuous control. We embed these denoisers into a plug-and-play framework, yielding a unified solver that spans the entire DP plane without retraining, and enables high-perceptual reconstructions at a fraction of the cost of posterior sampling methods. • Empirical validation. On CelebA and AFHQ inverse problems (inpainting, motion deblurring, super-resolution, Gaussian deblurring), our method matches or exceeds specialized baselines at both DP endpoints from a single trained model, and uniquely traces a smooth DP curve in between. D s , t D_{s,t} denotes the average denoiser (defined formally in Section 3.1 ). The lookahead t t controls the DP trade-off: at t = s t=s the denoiser is MMSE and PnP reconstructions concentrate at the posterior mean, which for this symmetric bimodal posterior lies between the two modes, yielding low distortion but poor perceptual quality; as t → 1 t\to 1 , the lookahead progressively restores the bimodal structure, recovering samples from both modes at the cost of higher distortion; details of this experiment are in Appendix B.4 .

sections.text: Recent works instantiate this proximal step with a learned denoiser D t D_{t} , yielding the iteration 𝐱 k + 1 = D t ​ ( 𝐳 k ) {\mathbf{x}}^{k+1}=D_{t}({\mathbf{z}}^{k}) ( Zhu et al., 2023 ; Martin et al., 2025 ; Mardani et al., 2024 ; Zilberstein et al., 2025 ; Renaud et al., 2024 ; Laumont et al., 2022 ; Laumont et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . This approach leverages implicit priors learned by generative models while retaining the flexibility of PnP for arbitrary forward operators. However, these methods typically optimize distortion, often at the expense of perceptual quality, resulting in over-smoothed reconstructions. In Section 3 , we show that replacing the instantaneous denoiser with an average denoiser associated to the flow-map enables continuous control over this tradeoff and improves perceptual quality.

sections.text: In this section we define and analyze the average denoiser associated to flow maps and its connection to the DP tradeoff (Section 3.1 ).

As expected, the average denoiser traces smooth, monotone curves in the DP plane: increasing t t improves perception (lower FID) at the cost of distortion (higher RMSE). The resulting curves exhibit the convex shape predicted by the optimal DP function. Unlike prior methods that provide only discrete or heuristic control, our approach yields a smooth and continuous parameterization of the DP frontier from a single trained model. We also observe that the traversal range increases with the noise level. For ξ = 0.1 \xi=0.1 , the range is narrow since the MMSE estimator is already close to the data distribution, whereas for ξ = 0.7 \xi=0.7 , the lookahead spans a wide range of operating points. This is consistent with Freirich et al. (2021) , as the perception gap P ∗ P^{*} grows with noise, allowing a larger tradeoff between distortion and perception. Fig. 30 illustrates this effect: as t t increases from s s to 1 1 , reconstructions transition from smooth averages to sharp, detailed images.

sections.heading: Variance restoration.
sections.text: A natural question is why increasing the lookahead improves perceptual quality. A simple explanation follows from the law of total variance: for any noisy observation 𝐱 s {\mathbf{x}}_{s} , we have Var ⁡ ( 𝐱 1 ) = Var ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐱 1 ∣ 𝐱 s ] ) + 𝔼 ⁡ [ Var ⁡ ( 𝐱 1 ∣ 𝐱 s ) ] \mathrm{Var}({\mathbf{x}}_{1})=\mathrm{Var}\!\big(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{s}]\big)+\mathbb{E}\!\big[\mathrm{Var}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{s})\big] . Since the second term is strictly positive, the MMSE estimator D s ​ ( 𝐱 s ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐱 1 ∣ 𝐱 s ] D_{s}({\mathbf{x}}_{s})=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{s}] has lower variance than the true data, i.e., Var ⁡ ( D s ​ ( 𝐱 s ) ) < Var ⁡ ( 𝐱 1 ) \mathrm{Var}(D_{s}({\mathbf{x}}_{s}))<\mathrm{Var}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}) . This variance gap leads to reduced contrast and over-smoothed reconstructions, and is precisely what the optimal DP estimator ( 9 ) corrects via interpolation. As the lookahead t t increases, the average denoiser progressively restores this variance, effectively traversing the same tradeoff within a single model. Fig. 2(b) supports this empirically: the relationship between variance ratio and FID is nearly identical across noise levels, suggesting that variance restoration underlies the observed perceptual improvements.

sections.heading: 4 Plug-and-play with average denoisers
sections.text: We now embed the average denoiser ( 10 ) into the PnP framework from Section 2.2 to solve general inverse problems with continuous DP control. Importantly, the DP interpretation applies at the level of the denoiser D s , t D_{s,t} , while the overall PnP solution reflects its interaction with the forward model. As a result, in general inverse problems, the lookahead controls a tradeoff that combines perceptual alignment with data-consistency effects, rather than exactly reproducing the denoising DP frontier.

sections.heading: Role of the renoising step.
sections.text: The stochastic renoising step is what makes the lookahead a DP knob in the inverse-problem setting. With renoising, D s , t D_{s,t} operates at its intended noise level s s , placing it in the regime where Theorem 1 characterizes its behavior, and the injected noise restores the sample diversity required at the perceptual end of the frontier. Without renoising, the iteration reduces to a fixed-point Tikhonov estimator and the lookahead degenerates into a bias-variance knob; we treat this case in Appendix D.4 .

sections.heading: Computational cost and connection to PnP-Flow.
sections.text: Algorithm 1 requires one forward pass through 𝐯 θ {\mathbf{v}}_{\theta} per iteration. The lookahead t t is merely a conditioning input, adding zero overhead and preserving efficiency over methods requiring ODE backpropagation or trace computations.

sections.heading: Consistency models and flow maps for inverse problems.
sections.text: Consistency models ( Song et al., 2023b ) learn to map any point on a probability flow ODE to its origin, enabling single-step generation. Consistency trajectory models ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025a ) generalize this to arbitrary pairs ( s , t ) (s,t) by learning the ODE solution operator. More recent works repurposed these models for controlled generation, either as guided samplers ( Sabour et al., 2025a ; Spagnoletti et al., 2025 ; Garber and Tirer, 2025 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) , as priors ( Gülle et al., 2026 ) , or for optimizing the noise initialization ( Mammadov et al., 2026 ) . Most recently, and concurrently to this work, Huang et al. (2026) also leverage flow maps for guidance, formulating reward-based generation as an optimal control problem and using the flow map for fast guided sampling. However, all these approaches primarily target accelerated sampling at a fixed operating point and do not provide explicit control over the restoration tradeoff. In contrast, we treat the lookahead t t as a continuous parameter, turning a single flow map into a family of estimators that spans the entire distortion–perception (DP) frontier.

sections.heading: Methods that traverse the DP plane.
sections.text: Recent approaches explore distortion–perception control by learning data-dependent flows between degraded and clean distributions. Inversion by Direct Iteration (InDI) ( Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023 ) and stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2024 ) learn flows from measurements to clean images, while Posterior-Mean Rectified Flow (PMRF) ( Ohayon et al., 2025 ) replaces the source distribution with an approximation of the posterior mean. These methods provide inference-time mechanisms for traversing the DP plane, either through integration schedules or through a scalar parameter that controls the interpolation between posterior-mean and perceptual reconstructions. However, they rely on supervised training with paired dat ( 𝐲 , 𝐱 ) ({\mathbf{y}},{\mathbf{x}}) and, in the case of PMRF, require an auxiliary model to estimate the posterior mean. Moreover, extending such approaches to handle different degradations generally requires collecting paired training data across those operators and scaling model capacity accordingly. In contrast, our approach learns a single unconditional flow map from clean images alone, whose lookahead parameter naturally induces a continuous family of denoisers. As a result, DP control is obtained from a single model without paired supervision, auxiliary networks, or retraining, and extends naturally to arbitrary forward operators through Plug-and-Play inference.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We evaluate all methods in two datasets: Celeba 128 × 128 128\times 128 and AFHQ 256 × 256 256\times 256 ; we also consider AFHQ-cats 192 × 192 192\times 192 . For each dataset, we train a flow map model v θ ​ ( 𝐱 , s , t ) v_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}},s,t) , parametrized by the Song UNet architecture ( Song et al., 2020 ; Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) , from scratch using the off-diagonal loss of LSD described in ( 5 ). More training details can be found in Appendix B.1 . We assess the reconstruction quality of the different samplers with mean squared error (in terms of PSNR = − 10 ​ log 10 ​ MSE \mathrm{PSNR}=-10\log_{10}\mathrm{MSE} ) and two perceptual metrics, LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and DISTS ( Ding et al., 2020 ) . In addition, we compute the FID Heusel et al. (2017) and KID Bińkowski et al. (2018) between ensembles of test set images and posterior samples. We compute the average of 100 samples, and for all the methods we consider Gaussian noise with σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 , unless random inpainting with σ = 0.01 \sigma=0.01 ; also, in Appendix C.2.2 we include an experiment with Poisson noise. We compared with recent methods that leverage pre-trained flow models, namely OT-ODE ( Pokle et al., 2024 ) , Flow Priors ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , D-Flow ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) , DPS-ODE ( Chung et al., 2023 ) and PnP-Flow ( Martin et al., 2025 ) , which corresponds to our proposed method for t = s t=s . For all the models, we performed a search grid of hyperparameters to obtain the best performance possible, and we use the same trained network for the prior/regularizer; we defer to Appendix B.2 for further details. We also include a comparison with baselines using a flow matching model as prior (a model trained without the second loss in ( 5 )), which can be found in App. C.4 .

sections.text: We evaluate on the following tasks: ( i ) (i) motion deblurring with random kernel genearted with the code 1 1 1 https://github.com/LeviBorodenko/motionblur and size 31 × 31 31\times 31 (CelebA) and 61 × 61 61\times 61 (AFHQ) and σ b = 1 \sigma_{b}=1 ; ( i ​ i ) (ii) random inpainting with 90 % 90\% missing pixels; ( i ​ i ​ i ) (iii) super-resolution ( × 4 \times 4 ); and ( i ​ v ) (iv) Gaussian deblurring, which are deferred to Appendix C.2 . Quantitative results are reported in Table 1 (with error bars in Appendix C.1 ), and visual results in Appendix C.5 and Fig. 5 . PnP-Flow with t = s t=s achieves the best or near-best PSNR across all four (dataset, task) settings, confirming that the average denoiser at small lookaheads behaves as a low-distortion estimator. At the other extreme, PnP-Flow with t = 1 t=1 achieves the best or near-best LPIPS DISTS and FID on every task; on inpainting, it matches DPS-ODE on FID while substantially improving LPIPS and DISTS. Competing methods either commit to a single operating point (DPS-ODE favors perception, D-Flow favors distortion) or fall short on both, whereas our approach attains both regimes from a single trained network. Beyond accuracy, PnP-Flow is also the fastest of the methods compared, as shown in Appendix B.3 . Lastly, we note that PnP-Flow with t = 1 t=1 is not uniformly the best perceptual method in all tasks. In particular, on Gaussian deblurring and super-resolution (in Appendix C.2 ), some baselines achieve better perceptual metrics. Nevertheless, increasing the lookahead from t = s t=s to t = 1 t=1 consistently shifts PnP-Flow toward the perceptual end of the DP spectrum, substantially improving FID, LPIPS, and DISTS relative to the distortion-oriented regime. We therefore view the main contribution not as identifying a universally optimal perceptual operating point, but as providing a principled mechanism for continuously traversing the DP tradeoff with a single trained model (see Appendix C.8 for further discussion).

sections.heading: 7 Discussion and limitations
sections.text: We introduced flow map denoisers, a generalization of the standard instantaneous denoiser that enables continuous, zero-shot traversal of the DP tradeoff. By reinterpreting flow maps as a continuum of average denoisers indexed by a lookahead parameter t t , we link flow maps to the theory of optimal DP estimators. This traversal is provably optimal for Gaussian targets and empirically validated for natural images. Embedded within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) solver, our approach enables inference-time control over restoration quality across diverse degradations, without retraining, paired data, or auxiliary models. Our approach has several limitations. First, the formal optimality result is restricted to the Gaussian case. While the image experiments in Section 3.3 suggest similar behavior more broadly, a general theoretical characterization remains open. In particular, understanding failure modes is an important direction for future work, as certain degradations can lead to non-monotonic DP behavior, like box inpainting in Fig 3 . Second, flow map models are more expensive to train than standard flow matching models and may underperform on pure distortion metrics such as PSNR. Third, while increasing the lookahead parameter consistently moves reconstructions toward the perceptual end of the DP spectrum, the resulting endpoint ( t = 1 t=1 ) is not always the best perceptual method. This suggests that the lookahead parameter should primarily be viewed as a mechanism for traversing the DP tradeoff rather than as a way of reaching the optimal perceptual operating point for every restoration task. The perspective in this work opens several directions for future work, borrowing ideas from the denoiser literature ( Milanfar and Delbracio, 2025 ) . Average denoisers could be trained directly via denoising objectives, such as SURE-based/consistency losses ( Raphan and Simoncelli, 2011 ; Daras et al., 2025 ; Tachella et al., 2025 ) . Extending the construction to more general noising processes, such as general restoration priors ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Elata et al., 2025 ) , is an additional natural next step. Lastly, our experiments are limited to pixel-space models (CelebA 128, AFHQ 256); extending the framework to latent-space and text-to-image settings is an important direction.

sections.heading: A.1 Flow Maps
sections.text: Consider a probability flow defined by the ordinary differential equation 𝐱 ˙ t = 𝐯 t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) , 𝐱 0 ∼ p 0 , \dot{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t}={\mathbf{v}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{t}),\quad{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim p_{0}, which transports samples from a simple distribution p 0 p_{0} to a target distribution p 1 p_{1} . The associated flow map 𝐗 s , t : ℝ d → ℝ d {\mathbf{X}}_{s,t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is defined as the solution operator of this ODE: X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 s ) = 𝐱 t , X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}}_{s})={\mathbf{x}}_{t}, i.e., it maps a point at time s s to its position at time t t along the flow trajectory. In particular, X 0 , 1 X_{0,1} directly maps samples from p 0 p_{0} to p 1 p_{1} , enabling one-step generation without numerical integration. A convenient parameterization of the flow map is given by X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝐱 + ( t − s ) ​ 𝐯 ​ ( 𝐱 , s , t ) , X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{x}}+(t-s)\,{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},s,t), where 𝐯 s , t {\mathbf{v}}_{s,t} can be interpreted as the average velocity between times s s and t t . In the limit t → s t\to s , this recovers the instantaneous velocity field: lim s → t ∂ t X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t ) , \lim_{s\to t}\partial_{t}X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t), which implies that 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t , t ) = 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t ) {\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t,t)={\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t) .

sections.heading: Characterization of the flow map.
sections.text: The flow map can be equivalently characterized in three ways: • Lagrangian form: ∂ t X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝐯 t ​ ( X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) , \partial_{t}X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})={\mathbf{v}}_{t}(X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})), which describes evolution along trajectories; • Eulerian form: ∂ s X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) + ∇ X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ 𝐯 s ​ ( 𝐱 ) = 0 , \partial_{s}X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})+\nabla X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})\,{\mathbf{v}}_{s}({\mathbf{x}})=0, which expresses conservation along the flow; • Semigroup property: X s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) = X u , t ​ ( X s , u ​ ( 𝐱 ) ) , X_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})=X_{u,t}(X_{s,u}({\mathbf{x}})), which encodes consistency across time intervals. These equivalent formulations provide the basis for learning flow maps in practice ( Boffi et al., 2025b ) .

sections.heading: Self-distillation framework.
sections.text: Instead of learning the instantaneous velocity field 𝐯 ( . , t ) {\mathbf{v}}(.,t) and integrating the ODE, flow map models directly learn 𝐯 ( . , s , t ) {\mathbf{v}}(.,s,t) by combining: • the diagonal loss in ( 2 ) enforcing 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t , t ) ≈ 𝐯 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t ) {\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t,t)\approx{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{x}},t) , • an off-diagonal loss enforcing consistency with one of the above three characterizations. Notice that throughout this work we used the LSD loss in ( 5 ), which is the one associated to the Lagrangian condition. This approach, known as self-distillation , allows training a single model that approximates the full flow map X s , t X_{s,t} without requiring a pre-trained teacher model.

sections.heading: B.1 Training details
sections.text: All models are trained unconditionally using the Flow Map objective ( Boffi et al., 2025b ) with the LSD loss ( 5 ).

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: We use the SongUNet Song et al. (2021) – a UNet with self-attention – with a base channel width of 128 and channel multipliers [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] [1,2,3,4] , giving four resolution scales. Self-attention is applied at spatial resolutions 16 × 16 16\times 16 and 8 × 8 8\times 8 . Each resolution level contains 3 residual blocks, dropout rate 0.1 0.1 , and a cosine resampling filter [ 1 , 3 , 3 , 1 ] [1,3,3,1] .

sections.heading: Time conditioning.
sections.text: The network is conditioned on two scalars ( α r , α t ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 2 (\alpha_{r},\alpha_{t})\in[0,1]^{2} representing the interpolation times of the source and target. Both are encoded with a positional (sinusoidal) embedding . Following Boffi et al. (2025b) , the two conditioning scalars are embedded as PE ⁡ ( α t − α r ) \mathrm{PE}(\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{r}) and PE ⁡ ( α r ) \mathrm{PE}(\alpha_{r}) , summed, and passed through a two-layer MLP with SiLU activations to produce a global conditioning vector injected into every residual block via adaptive group normalisation.

sections.heading: Loss weighting.
sections.text: For the off-diagonal term, we sample s , t s,t uniformly from { ( s , t ) : 0 < s < t ≤ 1 } \{(s,t):0<s<t\leq 1\} as detailed in Boffi et al. (2025b) . We follow Karras et al. (2024) and learn a per-sample uncertainty weight for the LSD loss, we attach a small network that outputs a scalar log-variance log ⁡ σ 2 ​ ( α r , α t ) ∈ ℝ \log\sigma^{2}(\alpha_{r},\alpha_{t})\in\mathbb{R} per training example. The network takes the concatenated pair [ α r , α t ] ∈ ℝ B × 2 × H × W [\alpha_{r},\alpha_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 2\times H\times W} and generate a scalar used to weight the loss as ℒ ∝ e − log ⁡ σ 2 ​ ℓ + log ⁡ σ 2 \mathcal{L}\propto e^{-\log\sigma^{2}}\,\ell+\log\sigma^{2} .

sections.heading: Datasets and resolution.
sections.text: • CelebA-HQ × 128 128\!\times\!128 Liu et al. (2015) : 202,599 images; 90% train split. • AFHQ × 256 256\!\times\!256 Choi et al. (2020) : 16,130 images; 90% train split. During training, 75% of the batch is used for the on-diagonal loss, while the remaining 25% for the off-diagonal one. Augmentation (horizontal flip, rotation, scaling, anisotropic scaling, translation) is applied with probability p = 0.12 p=0.12 .

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: All models are optimized with Adam ( Kingma, 2015 ) ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , ε = 10 − 8 \varepsilon=10^{-8} ) at a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with no learning-rate schedule.

sections.heading: B.2 Hyperparameters and baselines
sections.text: For all baselines, unless otherwise specified, we use σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 for Gaussian/motion deblurring and super-resolution, and σ = 0.01 \sigma=0.01 for inpainting. Blur kernel size is set to 61 for AFHQ and 31 for CelebA.

sections.heading: Flow-Priors ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) .
sections.text: We follow the original parameterization with guidance weight λ \lambda and step size η \eta . We use λ = 10 5 \lambda=10^{5} , η = 10 − 2 \eta=10^{-2} , and K = 1 K=1 inner iteration in all settings. The number of outer iterations is fixed to N = 100 N=100 .

sections.heading: D-Flow ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) .
sections.text: We tune the regularization parameter λ ∈ { 0.1 , 0.01 , 0.001 } \lambda\in\{0.1,0.01,0.001\} and the initialization blending parameter α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\} , retaining λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 and α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 . sections.text: We tune the initial time t 0 ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 , 0.4 } t_{0}\in\{0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\} and the step-size schedule γ ∈ { constant , t } \gamma\in\{\text{constant},\sqrt{t}\} . sections.heading: C.7 Performance as a function of the number of PnP iterations
sections.text: We study how the two endpoint lookaheads, t = s t=s and t = 1 t=1 , depend on the number of PnP iterations N N . Results for AFHQ are reported on super-resolution × 4 \times 4 (Fig. 24 ), Gaussian deblurring (Fig. 25 ) and box inpainting (Fig. 26 ); we also include for CelebA in Fig. 27 . The two regimes behave qualitatively differently. At t = s t=s , both RMSE and FID decrease monotonically with N N and plateau, consistent with the local-contraction analysis of Theorem 2 . At t = 1 t=1 , the perceptual trajectory is non-monotonic: FID drops sharply within the first few tens of iterations, reaches its minimum, and then drifts back up as N N continues to grow. The effect is most pronounced for Gaussian deblurring, where the best FID at t = 1 t=1 ( ≈ 11 \approx 11 at N ≈ 20 N\approx 20 ) is reached an order of magnitude earlier than the best FID at t = s t=s ( ≈ 23.5 \approx 23.5 at N ≈ 300 N\approx 300 ). This behavior is consistent with the lookahead-dependent contraction factor in Theorem 2 . The local Lipschitz constant L D loc ​ ( t ) L_{D}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t) grows with t t , reflecting the transition from a contractive MMSE estimator at t = s t=s to a less regular, perceptually-oriented estimator at t = 1 t=1 . RMSE remains well-behaved in both cases, indicating that the drift is along the perceptual axis. The practical takeaway is that the two endpoints call for different iteration schemes: the perceptual endpoint ( t = 1 t=1 ) is best run for fewer steps than the distortion endpoint ( t = s t=s ). The values of N N used in our main experiments (Appendix B.2 ) reflect this asymmetry. This behavior also explains why flow maps and consistency models are useful denoisers for solving restoration problem with few-steps as in ( Spagnoletti et al., 2025 ; Gülle et al., 2026 ) . The flow-map denoiser D s , t ​ ( 𝐱 ) = Λ ⁡ ( s , t ) ​ 𝐱 D_{s,t}({\mathbf{x}})=\Lambda(s,t)\,{\mathbf{x}} is not a proximal map: it operates at the intrinsic noise level σ s \sigma_{s} of the interpolant 𝐱 s {\mathbf{x}}_{s} , rather than the measurement noise σ obs \sigma_{\rm obs} . As the lookahead t t increases, c ⁡ ( t ) c(t) decreases and 𝐱 ⋆ ​ ( t ) {\mathbf{x}}^{\star}(t) moves toward the Wiener solution, reducing bias. sections.heading: Effect of renoising in the Gaussian setting.
sections.text: To isolate the role of the renoising step, we repeat the experiment with the full stochastic PnP iteration. While the deterministic case converges to a single Tikhonov solution, the stochastic iteration produces a distribution of estimates whose spread is largely independent of the step size λ \lambda . Across different λ \lambda , the sample clouds consistently exhibit meaningful variance and align with the geometry of the data distribution, even when the mean estimate remains over-regularized. This indicates that the renoising step, together with the denoiser, primarily controls the variance of the estimator, while λ \lambda governs its mean through the data-consistency update. As the lookahead increases, this variability is progressively amplified, yielding the distortion–perception behavior observed in the experiment.

Email: mmardani@nvidia.com Santiago Segarra Affiliation: Rice University Email: segarra@rice.edu Abstract Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ( 128 × 128 128\times 128 ) and AFHQ ( 256 × 256 256\times 256 ) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings. Code is available in https://github.com/nzilberstein/Flow-map-denoisers 1 Introduction Image restoration is a highly ill-posed inverse problem: a single degraded observation can correspond to a vast set of plausible clean images. Standard regression approaches that minimize mean squared error (MSE) approximate the conditional expectation ( Ongie et al., 2020 ) , achieving minimum distortion at the cost of over-smoothed reconstructions that lack fine detail. In contrast, posterior sampling techniques ( Kawar et al., 2021 ) produce realistic-looking solutions at the cost of higher distortion. This inherent compromise is formalized by the distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff ( Blau and Michaeli, 2018 ; Freirich et al., 2021 ) . Because the ideal balance between low distortion and high perceptual quality is strictly user-dependent, designing a single model capable of traversing the DP plane at inference time remains a central challenge in computational imaging. Most existing methods commit to a single operating point in the DP plane , either targeting minimum distortion through supervised regression ( Dong et al., 2015 ; Terris et al., 2026 ) , or minimum perception by leveraging recent generative models as priors ( Pokle et al., 2024 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Kadkhodaie and Simoncelli, 2021 ) to draw samples from the posterior. A few recent works based on data-dependent flow models aim to traverse the DP plane ( Ohayon et al., 2025 ; Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2024 ) , by explicitly interpolating between measurement-dependent estimators (e.g., the conditional mean) and the clean image. Unlike these approaches, which require external mechanisms, such as interpolation, discretization choices, or retraining, to move along the DP frontier, we show that this tradeoff is already implicitly encoded in the dynamics of flow maps. This raises the question of whether this behavior can be achieved without relying on solver choices, such as increasing the number of discretization steps. In this work, we propose a unified approach based on flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025b ; Boffi et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025b ) , which unifies all operating points along the DP plane within a single model. While prior work primarily uses flow maps to accelerate sampling ( Gülle et al., 2026 ; Sabour et al., 2025a ; Spagnoletti et al., 2025 ) , we instead leverage them to traverse the DP frontier . Our key observation is that the lookahead t t selects a point along a continuum of estimators—termed average denoisers —implicitly encoded within a single trained flow map, thus acting as a knob to control the characteristics of the restored image. This perspective reveals DP control as an intrinsic property of the learned flow map, eliminating the need for multiple models, auxiliary networks, or heuristic solver choices. This family spans the entire DP frontier, recovering the MMSE estimator at one extreme and approaching posterior sampling at the other. For Gaussian targets, we prove that this family spans the entire DP frontier, recovering the MMSE estimator at one extreme and approaching posterior sampling at the other, tracing the optimal DP curve ( Freirich et al., 2021 ) . While this exact theoretical correspondence strictly holds for Gaussian noise problems, we empirically observe similar behavior for natural images. When extending this approach to general, non-Gaussian inverse problems, traversing the lookahead serves as an approximation to the true DP frontier; here, the lookahead controls a tradeoff that combines perceptual alignment with data-consistency effects, rather than exactly reproducing the denoising DP frontier. By embedding these denoisers within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) framework ( Venkatakrishnan et al., 2013 ) , we leverage this property to obtain a versatile solver that effectively traverses the DP frontier across a wide range of inverse problems. Fig. 1 illustrates this behavior on a 2D Gaussian mixture model. Overall, our contributions are: • Flow maps as a continuum of DP estimators. We reinterpret flow maps as a family of denoisers indexed by a lookahead parameter t t , enabling continuous traversal of the DP plane with a single model. • Exact optimality in the Gaussian case. We show that this family recovers the optimal DP curve for Gaussian targets, establishing a direct link between flow maps and DP theory. • PnP reconstruction with continuous control. We embed these denoisers into a plug-and-play framework, yielding a unified solver that spans the entire DP plane without retraining, and enables high-perceptual reconstructions at a fraction of the cost of posterior sampling methods. • Empirical validation. On CelebA and AFHQ inverse problems (inpainting, motion deblurring, super-resolution, Gaussian deblurring), our method matches or exceeds specialized baselines at both DP endpoints from a single trained model, and uniquely traces a smooth DP curve in between. Consistency models ( Song et al., 2023b ) learn to map any point on a probability flow ODE to its origin, enabling single-step generation. Consistency trajectory models ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025a ) generalize this to arbitrary pairs ( s , t ) (s,t) by learning the ODE solution operator. More recent works repurposed these models for controlled generation, either as guided samplers ( Sabour et al., 2025a ; Spagnoletti et al., 2025 ; Garber and Tirer, 2025 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) , as priors ( Gülle et al., 2026 ) , or for optimizing the noise initialization ( Mammadov et al., 2026 ) . Most recently, and concurrently to this work, Huang et al. (2026) also leverage flow maps for guidance, formulating reward-based generation as an optimal control problem and using the flow map for fast guided sampling. However, all these approaches primarily target accelerated sampling at a fixed operating point and do not provide explicit control over the restoration tradeoff. In contrast, we treat the lookahead t t as a continuous parameter, turning a single flow map into a family of estimators that spans the entire distortion–perception (DP) frontier. Methods that traverse the DP plane. Recent approaches explore distortion–perception control by learning data-dependent flows between degraded and clean distributions. Inversion by Direct Iteration (InDI) ( Delbracio and Milanfar, 2023 ) and stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2024 ) learn flows from measurements to clean images, while Posterior-Mean Rectified Flow (PMRF) ( Ohayon et al., 2025 ) replaces the source distribution with an approximation of the posterior mean. These methods provide inference-time mechanisms for traversing the DP plane, either through integration schedules or through a scalar parameter that controls the interpolation between posterior-mean and perceptual reconstructions. However, they rely on supervised training with paired dat ( 𝐲 , 𝐱 ) ({\mathbf{y}},{\mathbf{x}}) and, in the case of PMRF, require an auxiliary model to estimate the posterior mean. Moreover, extending such approaches to handle different degradations generally requires collecting paired training data across those operators and scaling model capacity accordingly. In contrast, our approach learns a single unconditional flow map from clean images alone, whose lookahead parameter naturally induces a continuous family of denoisers. As a result, DP control is obtained from a single model without paired supervision, auxiliary networks, or retraining, and extends naturally to arbitrary forward operators through Plug-and-Play inference. 6 Numerical experiments We now focus on the numerical results. PnP-Flow with t = s t=s achieves the best or near-best PSNR across all four (dataset, task) settings, confirming that the average denoiser at small lookaheads behaves as a low-distortion estimator. At the other extreme, PnP-Flow with t = 1 t=1 achieves the best or near-best LPIPS DISTS and FID on every task; on inpainting, it matches DPS-ODE on FID while substantially improving LPIPS and DISTS. Competing methods either commit to a single operating point (DPS-ODE favors perception, D-Flow favors distortion) or fall short on both, whereas our approach attains both regimes from a single trained network. Beyond accuracy, PnP-Flow is also the fastest of the methods compared, as shown in Appendix B.3 . Lastly, we note that PnP-Flow with t = 1 t=1 is not uniformly the best perceptual method in all tasks. In particular, on Gaussian deblurring and super-resolution (in Appendix C.2 ), some baselines achieve better perceptual metrics. Nevertheless, increasing the lookahead from t = s t=s to t = 1 t=1 consistently shifts PnP-Flow toward the perceptual end of the DP spectrum, substantially improving FID, LPIPS, and DISTS relative to the distortion-oriented regime.
